newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Crumbling Khmer Rouge still seen force in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Crumbling Khmer Rouge still seen force in Cambodia.

text.p: As the military might of Pol Pot's feared Khmer Rouge starts to crumble, talk in the capital has turned to the political future of some of the group's leaders -- a topic that sharply divides Cambodia.

While it seems inconceivable to many that the people responsible for the 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime could win a place in mainstream politics, the prospect is increasingly likely, officials and political analysts said.
"I don't think this is the end of the Khmer Rouge at all," parliamentarian Son Chhay told Reuters.
"They're abandoning their fighting, but they're moving on to political struggle," he said.

On Saturday a senior Cambodian military official told a news conference that reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot was surrounded and under attack by 1,000 rebels from his own army in the Cambodian jungle.

Pol Pot, one of this century's most infamous figures, was holed up in rough jungle terrain about 20 km (12 miles) east of his northern stronghold of Anlong Veng with about 250 to 300 fighters and their families, said deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay.
His forces were holding at least three senior Khmer Rouge officials, including rebel government president Khieu Samphan, as hostages, he said.
Defence Chief Son Sen and 11 family members were said to have been brutally murdered at the order of Pol Pot before the rebels fled Anlong Veng.

The reports have been greeted with some scepticism, with many analysts wondering whether the episode may have been cooked up to differentiate the totally unpalatable Pol Pot, who will never be forgiven for his crimes, from his marginally less despised comrades.
More than one million people are estimated to have died through starvation, executions, hard labour and disease during the Khmer Rouge's disastrous experiment with total communism.
Either way, analysts agree the Khmer Rouge movement is splitting over whether or not to make peace, mirroring breaks within Cambodia's coalition government.

The unravelling of the guerrilla movement, which has been fighting the government since it reneged on a 1991 U.N. peace pact, began last August when Pol Pot's brother-in-law and former rebel foreign minister Ieng Sary broke with the movement.
Thousands of defections followed, and analysts believe fewer than 2,000 hard-line rebels remained in Anlong Veng when fighting reportedly erupted between guerrillas.

But even as the Khmer Rouge's once-feared military aparatus crumbled, the rebels were exploiting rifts between feuding co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who have competed to recruit defectors to their own sides.

Powerful former Khmer Rouge have won top government military posts and control over key territory. Khieu Samphan, who for years has served as the Khmer Rouge's more presentable public face, recently announced he wanted to form a political alliance with Ranariddh.
Ranariddh, running against Hun Sen's party in upcoming elections, has welcomed the prospect and favours pardoning for Khieu Samphan for any crimes committed during the Khmer Rouge regime.
While some within Ranariddh's political party have warned Khieu Samphan was a political liability, analysts note his strong nationalist, anti-Vietnamese stance has some appeal to Cambodians.
"Staggeringly, Khieu Samphan has some residual popularity," one foreign analyst told Reuters.
Assuming he comes out of the jungles around Anlong Veng alive, he may have a long political career ahead.

One analyst said it was interesting that the reports of the conflict in Anlong Veng emerged soon after Prime Minister Hun Sen said he would only consider an amnesty for him and other Khmer Rouge leaders if they fought Pol Pot.
"It may be Khieu Samphan is trying to appear to earn his political spurs," the analyst said.
Parliamentarian Ahmad Yahya told Reuters the Khmer Rouge are eyeing the 1998 elections even as they battle in the northwest.
"I believe that the strategy is to defect step by step until the end, and then they'll estabilish a political party and survive forever," he said.
